utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution is continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Madam President, can I have a few words, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I wish to express my deepest condolences on behalf of my colleagues and clients to all of our colleagues here from America here within this Tribunal for yesterday's tragedy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that when we were finishing yesterday, there was a question pending from the Bench for Mr. Donia, and before I begin, perhaps he could answer Your Honour's question. Just to remind the Court of those, Your Honour asked Mr. Donia whether or not the fact that this particular document regarding Variant A and B was not signed was unusual, whether in his prior experience all documents are or are not signed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me say that I have examined probably hundreds, rather than thousands, of party documents from the period, principally from the HDZ and SDS. Most documents that are in the custody of the preparer are signed and stamped simultaneously and so retained. Those that are distributed, the record is much less clear on whether there is a stamp and a signature. Quite typically there is the name of the addressee somewhere on the document. In this particular case of this document, there is, in fact, a number on the first page of the original, which is handwritten. This is the first -- the cover page of the B/C/S version of this document. If in fact the document is authentic, it would have been addressed to somewhere between 100 and 109 municipal boards, the number of municipalities, and this document that I have in front of me bears the handwritten number 96. So I would say that in form, this corresponds to at least some of the document that I've seen that are distributed to a substantial number of recipients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: We have on our photocopy slightly obliterated. I just see the bottom of a stroke which is 9 and 6. It is quite imperfect. Is that where it is, at the top, 96?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm looking at -- this is -- the number that I have up here is 00252738. This is the B/C/S version of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: You're looking at the front page where you see the numbers 100.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have number 96.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: May we have a look at your copy, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have another copy. I see that it's different. I have the number 100 also. I don't know if the Court wants to compare that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Yes. Ours bears the number 100, as does the Prosecutor's copy. So yours is different. Perhaps you want to explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honour, is that there are several different numbers that have been acquired which represent different numbering of this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Perhaps, Dr. Donia, you would want to look at the Court's copy to see if the rest of the pages are the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: I was suggesting that perhaps there is a need to see that the rest of the pages in that exhibit are the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd be glad to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, I'm just wondering. Yesterday, if I remember correctly, you mentioned that the copy of this document was one that you found in the archives from a certain magazine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So I'm wondering, therefore, how we therefore have two different numbered copies - 96 you have, and we have 100 - if you Xeroxed from the archives one copy. I'm a little bit confused on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding is that the Prosecution has acquired several different numbered documents, and these were provided for me. This is the first time I've seen the English -- authorised English translation of this document. My first encounter with this document was indeed in the newspaper published in March of 1992, and I was familiar with it in that version that is published only with no number indicated until a couple of months ago. If I may just take a minute and compare. Your Honours, I would just note that on the variant -- or the version 96, the number 96, in the original B/C/S there is some handwriting that appears on the third page that is not in the document numbered 100.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. We have not been disclosed these other copies of the documents: 96, 100, whatever. Can we have just a look at this? I mean, we cannot really object to this until we see the copies of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel. Thank you for pointing it out that you have different numbers as well. So maybe the Prosecution can explain, if there is any explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My understanding from my colleagues is that all versions have been disclosed to the Defence, but we can clarify that. To explain to the Court, there are several copies of this in the B/C/S language that were seized from various locations by the Tribunal or given to the Tribunal by various parties, so there are different versions. Apparently there were different copies with different numbers handwritten on them, depending on where that copy came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That is the problem we are having, because different counsel may have different numbers, the Court has a different number. So it's important that whatever document is exhibited, all the copies are from that document. Yes, because we also have a secondary problem, as always with these documents, that of translation. You have it in this language. You have it -- we may even go into looking at it, whether it was correctly translated. So that creates a lot of problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The copy that the Court has - and I don't know if counsel has it - is on the original in B/C/S -- the ERN number, the stamped number on the bottom, is 00184274 on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That number has been put -- is it original from the original document, or from the document which was found in the magazine, or is it a number put by your office?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's a number put by our office. I don't know if we want to stipulate to that for all purposes, but I think that every document that will submitted to the Court will have a sequential eight-digit number that we call the ERN number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, for the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Through the Evidence Unit it's given that number. Does counsel have that copy? Perhaps, given some of this confusion --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, perhaps I think the quick solution to this is as follows: that a copy of Professor Donia's document be extended to the Court, and if you have diverse other copies, to show a proliferation of this document at source, from wherever you collected it; then, if you have three or four or five such copies, then you make a bundle of those for whatever purpose you wish to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I've been informed that all copies -- all three versions have been distributed to the Court and counsel. Perhaps we don't take up the Court's time at this point. I can move on to my examination, and we can make sure later that it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can move on. Then we can come back to this at any other stage when you are ready, you have made sure that everybody has common copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, can you resume your PowerPoint presentation, and then I'm going to ask you to go forward on that. Can you please move forward to the maps on the next presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the screen is a map. It's labelled map 13 in the materials before the Court, and it's entitled "Bosanski Samac and the History of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, what does this map --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. May this map be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This map shall be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit P2M.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, what does P2M depict?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map is from the -- I took from the book of Lord David Owen, and it shows the situation in Bosnia and Croatia in early 1992. It specifically shows the position of the so-called United Nations protected areas, or UNPAs, at the end of the war in Croatia. And these areas which are lined - and if I may assert to the Court, I've coloured in these a little bit for highlighting - these areas were controlled by local Serbs and the JNA within Croatia. That defines, in a sense, the strategic problem that the JNA faced in the spring of 1992, because, as you can see, these areas are not contiguous east to west; so that the JNA - excuse me - the JNA had no way of establishing supply lines or communications between the eastern UNPA there around Vukovar and the western UNPA, with the city of Pakrac in the middle of it, other than to go through Bosnia. And in fact, the route lay logically through northern Bosnia, which was flat land and which was the by far easiest and shortest way to establish communications, first of all, between the areas of the Serb-controlled areas within Croatia to the west and Serbia to the east and, also, as the spring of 1992 moved forward, between Serb-controlled areas in Western Bosnia and Serb-controlled areas in Eastern Bosnia. So this map, I hope, explains the emergence of the Posavina Corridor just south of the Sava River, which emerged as a narrow strip of land which was strategically very important to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you show on the map with the arrow where the Posavina Corridor is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly in this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is Bosanski Samac in that corridor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And can you move forward to the next map, please. And what does this map depict?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, with some apologies, because this map is from 1995. It shows the disposition of military forces at the time of the Dayton Peace Agreement, and it specifically shows, as of 1995, basically toward the end of the war, the very narrow strip of land controlled by Serb forces, which then is the -- in fact the Posavina Corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May this map be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This map shall be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit P2N.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you move forward to the next map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And may this map of the northern area of Bosnia be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This map shall be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit P2O.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, does this depict the area of northern Bosnia that includes the Posavina Corridor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And is Bosanski Samac on this map? Can you please point it out?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have another map that has been distributed to the Court and counsel this morning. It is entitled "Assess Serbian Operational and Tactical Objectives." May that be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This map shall be marked P4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to put this on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours. May I have a word, please? My dear colleague, just tell me if your line of questioning would be related to the military issues or doctrine, military doctrine issues. I don't think that Mr. Donia is an expert for these kind of things. So just a suggestion to see, because in that case we are objecting. Mr. Donia is a historian, so he can speak about documents, about the -- well, his impression of certain events, but he cannot obviously speak about the manoeuvring, about the army, tactics, and all other things. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That is why you've been given the right to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's one of the reasons why you've been given the right to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's the reason. That's the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is this now on the computer? Your Honour, may this be displayed, please? It is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, can you explain what is depicted on this map?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think in -- let's say in very broad concept, with a misspelling here, it shows the link between east and west that is not true to the geographic situation, but it is an indication of a broad strategic imperative that the JNA faced in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you point out on this map where the Bosnian Krajina controlled by Serbian forces and the Croatian Krajina controlled by Serbian forces were at this time and how they were linked to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the date of this map? I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's presume in 1992. I'm not sure what the date of the map is, but at that time in 1992, can you show the situation of where Serbian forces were in the Croatian and Bosnia Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before that question is answered, because the witness did say he wasn't sure, the copy with the Court shows edition 2GSGS, October 1992. So we don't know whether that is the year this map was constructed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's correct. The map indicates the source.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time - and this is the fall of 1992 - the Serb forces controlled the area where I showed in the black and white map a moment ago. That is on the Croatian Krajina side here. And they controlled territory here and north of Bosanski Novi here. In Bosnia, by October 1992, they controlled the area from -- essentially from Banja Luka to the west and south to about here. So something like this area here was the area that they controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, did this corridor, or Posavina corridor, have strategic significance to the Serbian or particularly to the SDS authorities, and what evidence is there that they placed strategic significance in this corridor?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The significance of this Posavina corridor was first and foremost to the JNA, but it also had vital significance to SDS leaders because it was their link between the western-held territories and the Serbian republic and also to the Serbian-controlled territories in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a document that's been marked on the Prosecution exhibit list C39. It's entitled "Decision on Strategic Objectives of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina." May this document be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection to this exhibit only as far as the translation is concerned. The original of this document, the strategic objectives of the Serbian people, was given with a copy of the Official Gazette, and there is a date that is when this issue of the Official Gazette was published and the English translation only bears the date of when it -- of its adoption. So I would like to have the full translation entered into evidence as the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, I think you can deal with that, about what the Defence counsel has pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't know if we have the Gazette, the entire Gazette here. It's, I believe, a fairly lengthy document. My suggestion is that counsel can put that in on his cross-examination or through other witnesses, but all that is relevant right now to my examination of Dr. Donia is the one document. I agree with counsel that it did come from the Gazette.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but the date, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The date the Gazette was published?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Does that document in your hand have --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There is a date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It bears a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: -- of the decision -- the date it was -- of May the 12th, 1992. I think counsel's saying that this appeared in an Official Gazette which obviously was published after that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can agree -- we can agree on this. Can counsel tell the Court what date the Gazette bore?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the date on it -- I cannot tell you exactly. I don't have the copy on me. I think it was published about a year later, sometime in May 1993; in the original document, that is. But could I provide it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe we can have it admitted subject to your correcting the date, the date of the Gazette in which the document appeared. So we can go ahead and have a number and have it as an exhibit. MR. LUKIC [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit P5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May this exhibit be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There are copies also to be distributed to the Court and counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Donia --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: First asking you about point number 1 of this decision. Does this indicate -- it indicates demarcation of a state separate from the other two national communities. Can you explain what your understanding is of what that meant? What are the other two national communities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the original, but this says "ethnic communities." I assume it pertains to the Croatian and Muslim peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the third point of the decision, can you -- it indicates that the strategic objective is the establishment of a corridor -- excuse me, in the second point, a corridor between Semberija and Krajina. What is Semberija and Krajina? What corridor are we talking about there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Semberija, if I -- I still have my one map up here, Semberija is off to the east of Brcko, off to the right of this map. So the area of Semberija is east of the Posavina Corridor of which we have been speaking, and the Krajina refers to the western territories which were then under control of the Bosnian Serbs. So this document, therefore, affirms, actually, a decision reached earlier to set up a corridor for the purposes of linking those two eastern and western territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, your report deals with the outbreak of hostilities in the area of Bosanski Samac. And I'm not going to go over that. I do have one other map I would like to have displayed and ask you to comment on that, putting the attack on Samac in context with what was going on in other areas of northern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May this map which is entitled "Outbreak of Hostilities in 1992" be given a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but we have received actually two pages of the document C39, and the other page has nothing to do with the first page. It's just some sort of a letter from Ministry of Defence to Secretariat of Banja Luka, Sanski Most, from May 2, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I only put in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That is actually visible, even though we don't know the language. You can see the titling is different. So can we remove this paper?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Please. I only marked the one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Because it gave us the impression that this was the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not the translation. It was concerning the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is concerning the course and a veterinary exam, something like that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we'll hand the second page back to the Registry. Before the number is given, any objection to this Outbreak of Hostilities in 1992 map? I see no objections, so can we have the numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we don't see the map. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's on the screen, on the video evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But counsel should also -- you have copies already? Does counsel have copies already?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We received it yesterday, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This map titled "Outbreak of Hostilities in 1992" shall be marked as Prosecutor's Exhibit P6.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do have an objection to this map. I'm sorry. I was just trying to find out which map was it with the TV. Actually, we don't know exactly if those are the exact dates, because we were never -- it was never actually -- can I talk in Serbian? I'm sorry. It would be much easier for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Because the interpreters are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The thing is, there are certain dates on this map concerning alleged starting times for fighting in certain places in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Until now, we have only been familiarised with documentation. And, moreover, in a joint statement of the Prosecution and the Defence, we accepted the 17th of April as the date of commencement of hostilities in Bosanski Samac. As for these other dates, we really cannot either confirm them or have any information as to whether these dates are correct or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What counsel is, in fact, saying is that other than Bosanski Samac, which is given 17th April, the rest of the places mentioned -- the dates on the rest of the places mentioned were never given to the Defence, and you can neither confirm, as you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are seeing them for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Prosecution, are we planning to deal with all these other dates, or are we restricted to 17th April, Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We are planning to deal with all the other dates. I believe that the map, with the dates, was disclosed to the Defence before. They don't have to agree to those days, but it is a matter of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: At what stage was this map disclosed to the Defence? When?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps it's better if one of the attorneys that were involved in the disclosure to answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To answer, yes. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm informed it was disclosed on the 17th of February, 1998; four years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Defence counsel? MR. DI FAZIO: And, and, and, and admitted into evidence by order of the Court, the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The pre-trial -- MR. DI FAZIO: -- the Pre-Trial Chamber in 1999. So it's a long time ago. But it's been given, and that might account for the fact that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to know if all other Defence counsels have had this map with all the places, the dates. Because if they are common, then that means counsel may have missed this particular -- MR. DI FAZIO: If I may also add, apparently it's been disclosed not once, but three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. Maybe you have an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Madam President. I think we can very easily resolve this matter. All these dates are to some extent -- yes, sorry. Madam President, speaking about the dates, you can imagine that the other dates might be a matter for interpretation and, I would say, agreement between two parties in other cases. I particularly don't see any problem. Maybe our learned colleague could provide us with the non-disputed facts; for example, if he is speaking about Prijedor, from Prijedor case, or let's say Bijeljina or Brcko, and the other cases. So we could move on. I mean, it's not some important thing to waste time about it, so in due course we could arrange that and inform accordingly this Honourable Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel who placed the objection, is that satisfactory to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, just for the record, I got this map disclosed yesterday. For the first time I have seen this in the documents. Actually, the situation is that I got into this case on August 9, 1999. It might happen that there is some misunderstanding between me and the former counsel. I cannot exclude that, and I'm sorry if I caused trouble. But still, I got this map introduced yesterday. But in order to -- efficiency of these proceedings, I will accept this solution that my learned colleague offered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's better. Then we can move on, and then if you have any evidence later on --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm satisfied with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Donia, does this map indicate that the attack on Samac occurred in fairly close proximity to attacks on other towns in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are you familiar with course of events that occurred particularly in Northern Bosnia regarding attacks by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you explain how those attacks related time-wise, what the relationship was time-wise between those attacks?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the word "takeover" is better than "outbreak of hostilities," which the map is, in my view, not accurately entitled. But the attacks on takeovers of these northern Bosnian towns all took place within about 40 days, one town at a time, essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Following the Court's instructions, I believe the other materials are covered in the report. Thank you for Your Honours' patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination. Any cross-examination? Before we start, I would like to know whether -- how many Defence counsels are going to cross-examine the witness, or whether you've agreed that only one will cross-examine on behalf of everybody, since the evidence of the witness covers the whole scenario.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam President. Could we have just a few seconds to consult?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Madam President, in order to speed up proceedings, we have decided to split in four. So each Defence team will have a certain portion of the cross-examination, and we can go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So can we have the first counsel start, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Donia. My name is Catharine Baen. I think we met yesterday. I am one of the lawyers for the Defence, obviously. I represent, along with my co-counsel, Mr. Zecevic, the defendant Milan Simic in this case.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And I wish you good morning again and I hope that your family and your friends are okay back in the States.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are, and I wish you the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. What I'd like to do right now is refer you to your C.V., which is a portion of P1, I believe, Exhibit P1 for identification purposes. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And I don't know why we didn't go through this yesterday, but I want to go over it for just a second just to sort of get an idea of your background and your experience and who you are. I see that you worked for Merrill Lynch for about 20 years in the financial industry. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: In fact, you started in Houston, Texas, which is my home. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And it shows here that -- I believe you retired or you quit working for ^ Merrill Lynch in the year 2000, last year?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I retired last year, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And you're not working right now in the financial industry at all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct; I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. In fact, aren't you associated with or have formed some foundation in California entitled the "Donia Vakuf Foundation"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And I see on your C.V., Dr. Donia, that you speak several languages. You speak Serbo-Croat. I don't speak Serbo-Croat. Being from Texas, I barely speak English. So I didn't even know what kind of word "vakuf" was, so yesterday I went to the official interpreter for the Court and asked him what "vakuf" meant, and I was informed that it is some sort of land. It's a Muslim word that has Turkish origins that has to do with religious land; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Its origin, actually, is Arabic. And in --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Hold on just one --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ottoman --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: My question, actually is the word. The origin, yes, Turkish, Arabic. My question is: Is it a word that Muslims use designating certain lands for religious purposes, to make it easier for you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means a foundation. And the resources that make up a foundation of a vakuf can be land; they can be some sort of fund; they can be a shop, or any other income-producing economic entity.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. Just so we're clear, though, I've looked in the dictionary also, and the definition I received, the Muslim definition: Heritage for general, religious, and humanitarian purposes, with the aim to build and uphold mosques, schools, public libraries, hospitals, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see counsel for the Prosecution on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I object to counsel testifying to the Court. If she has questions for the witness, she may do so, but I believe she is offering opinion testimony that I don't get a right to cross-examine her on, or the dictionary.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I believe -- I mean, I'm asking questions that may be too long, but in cross-examination I'm giving him the information. I'm going to ask him whether he agrees or doesn't agree with it. And the dictionary is -- dictionaries are something that are objective criteria -- objective forms of information. So I'm just asking him questions about the terminology that's generally known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, as long as you stick to what is relevant. I know that counsel can challenge the witness on anything that is in the report, including the C.V., but we better move to what is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Anyway, I don't want to belabour this at all. Just the point is, right now, since you've retired, you've formed a foundation that has this word that Muslims use to designate certain land; fair enough?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. That's not the -- I, first of all, don't know of any language called Muslim, so I don't know what dictionary you acquired the word from.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Just for your information, it's "Vocabulary of Foreign Words and Expressions," Prosveta, 1970. Also another dictionary. I can't pronounce the word. B-r-a-t-o-i-t-u-b-k-l-a-i-c, dated 1982.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. But, Counsel, why are we wasting so much time on this? Because we all know that language evolves --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- the use of terms changes --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Especially in the last three years.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: The whole point I'm just trying to make - we will move on - is: This is not an English word. Okay?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right; it's not an English word.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And the purpose of your foundation is what?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of the foundation is to assist educational, academic, and humanitarian activities in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And recently you have helped some organisation preserve Bosniak literature in Sarajevo; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: The organisation spelled C-u-p-r-i-j-a?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cuprija is the name of a group of librarians in the United States and the former Yugoslavia who are working to reconstitute the collections of the national and university library in Sarajevo. It has nothing to do with Bosniak literature.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So if the web page for that organisation says that's what they're doing, is trying to protect collections of Bosniaca, then that's not correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you misinterpret the word "Bosniaca." "Bosniaca" was the term developed after the destruction of the national and university library in 1992, as in -- it was taken after the form Judaica or whatever, to characterise all works that were in that library.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. So my first question, my question, "Did you help this organisation," the answer is yes, then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you. While we have your C.V. out, I'd like for you to please turn to the section about your prior testimony before this Tribunal, your prior expert testimony.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And before we move into that, if someone asked you what sort of expert you're designated as here for your testimony, is it as an expert in history of the area or are you an expert in the history and the military strategy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I identify myself as, and I believe the Court looks at me as, a historical expert on all aspects of history.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So you are considered to be an expert in military strategy of the area as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The question can't be answered. It depends on who is considering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: That's a different question on strategy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: A historian can study what happened, how the military was moving and all that, so he need not be a military expert himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: That's why I was asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So you're not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a historian, and there's a great deal of military strategy that makes up history. And I've written on some of that and studied some of it, and of course over a very long period of time, from, you know, Middle Ages forward, but it certainly is a part of history.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. Looking at your C.V., it looks as though you were involved in three different cases in front of the Tribunal dating back to 1997. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And how many hours would you say you spent being involved in all your work here in the Tribunal for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it's hard to say. I couldn't give you an estimate really of hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Hundreds? Thousands?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, something -- maybe several hundred would be close, but something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And in these three different cases in which you were involved, you testified in one, correct, the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I testified in the Blaskic case, and I testified in the Kordic and Cerkez case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So you testified in Court in all three cases?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not testify in Court in the Kvocka case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And going through these cases, the Blaskic case, that involved a Croat, is that correct, the defendant?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And the Kordic case also involved a Croat defendant; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And the last case you mentioned, the Prijedor case, that involved Serb defendants; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And so you have never testified in any of them -- the Muslim Prosecution here before the Tribunal [sic]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Never been asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: That's correct, you've never been asked; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can leave your C.V. -- or your report for a moment and move to just a general but very brief conversation about your expertise as an historian in this area. You got your Bachelor's degree in history back in 1967; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And I myself got my Bachelor's degree in history, as well as my co-counsel, before I went to law school. And I remember - and I don't know if you'll agree with me - that back when you're studying history and when you study the discipline or art of history, sometimes there are a lot of arguments about opinions on certain events. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: In fact, that's sort of the whole gist of history, is you gather as much information as you can about a certain topic and then you analyse it and you come up with your own opinion; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ideally that would be the way the process works, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And there are very well-respected historians in many areas who have completely differing opinions about events and their causes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: But the idea is to get as much information as possible; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Looking at your -- actually, let's look at P1 again, your report. We don't even have to look at it. As I looked at it, I found that there were 178 footnotes in your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And in looking through those and analysing them with my co-counsel, we found that of those 178 footnotes, 7 came from Serbian authorities, 6 came from Serbian newspapers, compared to 65 that came from Muslim and Croatian authorities, and 25 newspaper articles from one newspaper from Sarajevo during the wartime, and 13 documents supplied to you by the Tribunal. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're better than I am at assigning ethnicity to the authors of those works and documents. I couldn't attest to the ethnicity of all those publications or papers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: That's fair enough. But would you argue with me that that's incorrect? Would you assume with me that that is correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The question isn't clear. He indicated he did not know the ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Would counsel be on your feet, please, if you're objecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. I felt the question was impossible to answer, because he indicated he did not know the ethnicity, and then counsel asked him if he agreed with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel. You have understood the objection, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I do. I'll try to make it easier.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Would you agree that the majority of the sources for your report don't come from Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it impossible to split the ethnicities in such a way to say that. No, I couldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. The same thing then. Let's turn to your book entitled "Bosnia and Herzegovina: A Tradition Betrayed" that you wrote with John Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honours would like me to have this marked, or may I ask the witness questions about his book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because it is a book, you can ask questions even if it is not yet marked. We will see whether or not it will be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Turning to your book and going to the bibliography of the time period in question in this case, on page 295, the Bosnian war period -- and you wrote this book in 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: It was published in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And in looking in the sources -- actually, it looks like of all nine sources, most of them are American sources. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That bibliography contains only English-language sources. I believe there is a note at the top that it is not intended to be a list of sources but rather a -- basic readings on similar topics.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: For the Bosnian war period 1992 and on, it says. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you leave the book, do you have a copy for the Court, for the Registry?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: You can have this copy, I guess. I only have one copy, Your Honour, and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because, you see, the point is any document discussed by a witness, even if given an ID number, it has to be kept by the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: That's fine. That's why I was asking the question if you wanted me to have it marked and given to the custody of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Now I see that it is necessary to have a ID. That's why I'm asking do we have a copy for the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: We can have this copy, Your Honour, and then if we need to refer to it later in the trial, we'll just ask for the use of it. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But it will remain with the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: May I have this marked then, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. An ID number only, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This book shall be marked as ID1/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get down to what this case is all about, and I won't have many more questions for you at all. I know you'll probably be disappointed. Bosanski Samac. I'm wondering, have you ever visited the town or municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Have you read the indictment with respect to this Prosecution, Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: When did you read that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About May of this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: You were asked to be an expert in this case in May?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And when did you compile your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since then. Between May and, I guess, August 1st.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. Bosanski Samac. Turning to your report, paragraphs 161 and 162 of P1, please. This is the section with respect to ethnic cleansing, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And paragraphs 161 and 162, you are outlining and, I guess, sort of summarising the special report to the UN by Mazowiecki; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And in paragraph 161, you state that: "After visiting the region in August and October of 1992, Mazowiecki and those accompanying him reported that `massive and systematic violations of human rights' were underway in BH, conducted principally in areas that were under Serbian control." Is that what you stated in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And then going on in paragraph 162, the term "ethnic cleansing" is defined according to Mazowiecki's report, and you -- you refer to different portions of the report where Mazowiecki went out into the country, visited certain areas, monitored them, and determined whether or not there had been ethnic cleansing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And do you have a copy of Mazowiecki's report with you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the courtroom. I believe I have it with me in Holland.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I do have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, also, I apologise. I don't know if this was marked as a Prosecution exhibit earlier or if you'd like for me to get another identification number for purposes of my cross-examination. Whatever the Court would like for me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is the document called?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: This is the UN report done by Mazowiecki that the doctor refers to in his expert report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I wonder whether the Prosecution -- whether it was one of the documents dealt with on discovery. Is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, but it hasn't been marked for court purposes. It needs an ID number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So, Counsel, you would like to examine the witness on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to have this marked for identification purposes, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number? ID only, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This shall be Defence ID2/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: In our document identified as 2/1, which is Mazowiecki --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please always use the prefix "ID."

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: ID number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, so that the record shows that this is a document which has just been identified, not produced.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes. I totally understand, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: In our document ID number 2/1, which is the UN special report by Mazowiecki -- since you don't have your report, I'm going to summarise. And if you disagree with what I have to stay, then I'll know you'll let me know. What Mazowiecki does is he goes through many different areas in the countries, as I mentioned earlier, and there's monitoring done and there's a determination as to whether or not there's been ethnic cleansing done; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he interviews a number of people in the region.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Correct. As a matter of fact, he interviews a lot of people, and he does in-depth interviews.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And is there anywhere in this report that the municipality of Bosanski Samac is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: In fact, to your knowledge, Bosanski Samac was not monitored by Mazowiecki; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He certainly does not mention it in his report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Well, his report is very detailed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's -- he highlights, I think, four or five places, and Bosanski Samac is not one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Right. The town of Bosanski Samac is not mentioned and the municipality is not mentioned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: In fact, the only place that's mentioned in his report that's geographically in the area of Bosanski Samac is - and I'm going to probably say this wrong; I'm learning the languages - the camp in Batkovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. And as a matter of fact, in his report, he says that this camp in Batkovic, which I believe is mentioned by the Prosecutors in opening or in some documents in this case, contained approximately 1.000 Muslim prisoners at the time of the visit and that the prisoners did not complain of ill-treatment and in general appeared to be in good health. Is that what he said about the camp in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me. I'll certainly take your word that that's in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I'll be happy to let you read it or -- would you like to read it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to see the context in which it's discussed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: It's paragraph 29. And I have some more questions about that. We'll continue. If you'll read the first part, and then I can get my copy back because it's the only copy I have.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paragraph 29 reads: "The camp in" --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Sir, please let me ask the questions. You'll have a chance to fully explain everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let the witness read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I just wanted to finish my questioning.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The camp in Batkovic contained approximately 1.000 Muslim prisoners at the time of the visit, housed in two storage buildings. The prisoners did not complain of ill-treatment, and in general, appeared to be in good health. However, they sleep on straw bedding, on the floor of cavernous, unheated buildings where living conditions will become intolerable as cold weather arrives."

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. Can I have the document back, please? Doctor, there's no mention of any beatings? Were there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: No mention of any sexual assault?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: No mention of any killings?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Let's go back to your book for a moment with respect to Bosanski Samac. Is there any mention of Bosanski Samac in your book whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And this strategic -- excuse me, "very strategic area" you mentioned of the Posavina Corridor, is there any mention of the Posavina Corridor in your book?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there's a mention of the Posavina, but I don't know that the corridor is addressed specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Well, shall we get out the index to look for Posavina to see whether or not it's there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be. I don't recall. It could be.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: If I told you I read the index and I didn't find Posavina anywhere in there, would you accept that as true?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. In your PowerPoint presentation, there was a slide that you prepared with the breakdown of the nationality in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991, where you broke down the Serbs, Croats, Muslims, Yugoslavs, and others; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And you divided Bosnia and Herzegovina versus just the municipality of Bosanski Samac; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And when you did this breakdown -- actually, when you're referring to Bosanski Samac, you're talking about the municipality, not the town?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the statistical population tables that I prepared both in the PowerPoint presentation and in the report, the unit of analysis is Bosanski Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Exactly. So from reading the indictment, as you said you did, you understand that most of the allegations in this case occurred in the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. And you understand that the town is -- out of a total population of almost 33.000 in the municipality, this little town is about 6.000 people, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So when you did this breakdown for the whole municipality, when you did the ratio of the ethnicities, that ratio doesn't necessarily represent the breakdown for the town of Bosanski Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. And so you have no idea -- I was going to talk to you about the numbers in the breakdowns of the towns itself. But you have no idea what that breakdown is, do you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I looked at it and recall that it was very mixed in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: You didn't really find it significant enough to put in a slide, did you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I chose not to put it in that slide because I was simply trying to compare the single municipality to the overall Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. I'm not trying to quarrel with you. Just for some reason it just -- it's not in your PowerPoint presentation; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So if I told you that there were a little over 2.000 Muslims in the town itself, would you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't, without consulting a source, agree or disagree. I would find it unsurprising, since the towns were frequently mixed and the proportion of Muslims in that particular area is often quite urban.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: So if I told you that, you're not going to just totally disagree with that or dismiss that idea; right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Where were you raised? Were you raised in a city or small town? You were raised in Michigan; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Were you raised in a small town?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the eye of the beholder, but it was Kalamazoo, Michigan, a town of about, I guess, 50,000.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay. So that's really not small. I mean, compared to -- I was raised in a town about the same size of Bosanski Samac, a farming community, and I consider that to be a small town. You would too, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Did you ever -- when you started preparing your expert opinion for this case, did you ever -- since you hadn't been to Bosanski Samac, did you have anybody go to the archives of Bosanski Samac to get information for you so you could get accurate information about the town?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And you never interviewed any witnesses with respect -- you never interviewed any witnesses from Bosanski Samac, did you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: In fact, the -- several -- I dare say many of the witnesses in this case were actually childhood friends and have grown up and worked with these defendants in this case. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see counsel for the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Counsel's arguing the case and not asking --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you repeat your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Counsel is arguing her case and not asking questions of the historical expert. It's not a proper question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: It's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You see the point?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I'm almost done, Your Honour. I'm just testing his knowledge of Bosanski Samac. And I think the point's been made, and I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Never met any of the defendants in this case; you never interviewed any witnesses; you've never been to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And one more question before I sit down. I forgot to ask you: When was this foundation, the Donji Vakuf foundation, founded? What year?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 1997.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: And you did your report on this case -- you compiled it in June of this year?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the end of May until August 1st, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The next counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam President, I will be speaking and asking my questions in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Donia, can we say that Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a geographical concept, was defined even before the arrival of South Slavs into this area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that within the group of South Slavs, as you call them in your own work and which is an accepted term, there were members of tribes of Serbs, Croats, Macedonians, Montenegrins, Bulgarians and other peoples?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Would you also agree with me that the Serbs had their own state in the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, and the fourteenth centuries?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree that the Serbian Orthodox Church, as a Christian church, was established in the thirteenth century, namely by Rastko Nemanjic, the patriarch?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In your presentation, you stated that during the rule of Tsar Dusan, the Serbian Empire comprised also parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that with the expansion of the empire, the Serbian Orthodox Church expanded as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we now also agree that even at that time, the Serbian nation came into being in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many scholars would argue that that is the case. My own feeling is it depends largely on what one uses as a definition of nation, Serbian nation, and depends on the specific evidence being accused for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could we then say that it was then, for the first time, that the awareness appeared with the members of the South Slavs, who accepted the Orthodox Church as their own religion, the awareness that they were Serbs? Would it be true to say that they felt as Serbs back then, if for no other purpose than for the sake of the privileges that gave them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't know much about the extent of that identity, but I would say that for some people, many people, yes. The answer is yes, a Serbian consciousness did exist at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You mentioned the Bosnian Church. Could we agree - and I don't see why we should not - that the Bosnian church was also a Christian church?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I think there is no reason why we shouldn't also agree that Islam appeared in the Balkans, and especially in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Macedonia, in the fifteenth century, and perhaps even later, but let's make it fifteenth century.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In the part in which you talk about the Ottoman Empire, is it true that a lot of administration and a lot of soldiers arrived who were in power while not being of Slav origin?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that depends on the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In which way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- there was very little of that in the geographic area of present-day Bosnia. There was some. And I think more non-Slavic soldiers and administrators arrived basically to the more eastern areas of the Ottoman Empire, Eastern Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that on the territory of the present-day Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the time when the Ottoman Empire conquered this territory, Serbs and Croats populated it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that only Serbs constituted the population there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: But just a moment ago you said that Serbian awareness existed even then, during Tsar Dusan and the ascent of the Serbian church. Would it be true to say that at least partially Serbs constituted the population, at least in those areas which fell under the empire of Tsar Dusan?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're talking about Tsar Dusan, that's -- I thought you asked there a question about the Ottoman Empire and its conquest of the area Bosnia at the time of the conquest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My question -- my last question was precisely that. And now in your answer you say that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbs and Croats were not the population. I'm now asking you which of the nations, the peoples, the tribes from the group of south Slavs did populate this area.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And excuse me. You answered that those were Serbs, Croats, Montenegrins, Macedonians, Bulgarians, and so on. Which of those five or six peoples did populate the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you'll see in my paper that I indicated that the tribal character of the peoples who migrated -- it lost its tribal character in that time. May I answer, sir? May I answer your question? And consequently, to assume the continuity from the sixth or eighth century until the fifteenth I don't believe is a necessarily a valid assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: It is precisely because you claim in your presentation that on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Middle Ages, Serbs and Croats did not live. That is precisely the reason for my question. You are trying to tell us that some people were living there without any national identity. South Slavs is not a national identity, in our eyes. In that group of south Slavs that arrived first, there were more narrow groups which had all the markings of nationhood. Just one more thing: You also said - and I would just like you to confirm this, if we can agree on this - that Serbs migrated into parts of Vojna and Bosnian Krajina, Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not specifically agree with your formulation. It's clear that the people who migrated to the Vojna Krajina and the Bosnian Krajina were Serbian Orthodox migrants. They are viewed by many scholars as having been Wallachs. The Habsburg decree regularising their status is called the Wallach decree. I don't propose to resolve that question of identity. I don't know. But there is no unanimity on the fact that they would be Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I wonder if we are going to agree on this now. Is it true that the term "Wallachs" was a common term among Croats for Serbs, and also among Bosnians relating to Serbs, back then and perhaps to this day?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps more to this day than back then. I think the term had a much more broad application at the time that the migrations took place, because some of the Wallachs were -- or supposed Wallachs were Catholics. So it isn't clear that those terms, "Wallach" and "Serb," are synonymous or were synonymous at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who called Catholics Wallachs? I don't know this.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- there's a whole literature on the question of who the Wallachs were. I'm trying to think of who has addressed that question specifically. It's principally Ottoman historians who deal with their identity, and I can't give you a name right now, but many scholars will take the position that Wallachs developed a national identity based on their religious affiliation in the course of the nineteenth century.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, it's 11.00. It's 11.00. Can we take our break? We shall resume at 11.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Cross-examination is continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, since we couldn't agree whether these were the Serbs who were being settled in the area of Vojna Krajina, can we say at least that they were Christian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did the Ottoman administration, which consisted of Vezirs [phoen], Beys, Pashas, Agas [phoen], and members of the Islamic religious community, implement certain zulum, as we call it locally, which means certain taxes and other things?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After the first Serbian uprising in 1804, did Serbia become one of the carriers of the idea of liberation among the people of south-eastern Europe who were under the Ottoman rule?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that the Serbian people in the Nevesinje uprising in 1875 delivered the coup de grace to the Ottoman Empire in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that was a coup de grace to the Ottoman Empire in the Balkans. It set in motion a train of events which led to the transfer of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Ottoman to Austrian control.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We know about the Berlin Congress and all that. What was the contribution, then, of this great uprising, which is known as the Nevesinje uprising, in acceleration of these processes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just take issue with the label. It's called the Bosnian uprising in the Serbian literature, and it was -- it served to highlight the inadequacy of Ottoman administration in that part of the world, and particularly the tensions at that time between Ottoman rule and the status of the Christian peasants in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was the status of Christian peasants in Bosnia difficult, hard?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: With annexation of Bosnia by Austro-Hungarian Empire, those who -- both the Muslims and Serbs remained dissatisfied with it and, so far as I know, they joined forces to try to resist this by taking up arms. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think you're referring to the occupation, not the annexation. The occupation was 1878. The annexation was 1908. And at the time of the occupation in 1878, yes, you're correct; the Bosnian Serbian Orthodox or Serbs, whatever you wish to call them, and Muslims, combined --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In your report, you mentioned Petar Petrovic Njegos, the bishop, and can we agree that he, in addition to being the ruler of Montenegro, was also a priest; that is, a bishop?
