utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that he was a man of letters, that he was a philosopher, a thinker?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I hope that we will also agree that by nationality, he was Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In your report, you stated that in the "Mountain Laurel," there is -- that it has the character of Serb patriotism. In addition to that, can we agree that this was a literary work whose author is a priest who is Christian, who is trying to defend Christianity against Islam, which had spread in that area?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I hope that you will agree with me that it is an obligation of a man of church to defend his own faith from the influence of other faiths.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a judgement I would not want to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Because the Ottoman Empire stayed the most in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would you agree with me that with the emergence of Serbia and Montenegro as Christian states, some of the population from those states migrated to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the word "Muslim" in Arabic means a member of Islamic faith?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned the young Bosnia, or mlada Bosna, and you said that its members were young Serbian intellectuals. Do you know that there were also Muslims and members of other ethnic groups among the members of this group?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Does the name Mustafa Golubovic mean anything to you? He was tried together with Gavrilo Princip and other accused after the assassination of 1914.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him only by name, yes; only that he was one of the defendants.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can we agree that in 1918, the kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, the so-called SHS kingdom, the constituent peoples brought in their national identity rather than territory and that it was only Serbia and Montenegro who also contributed their statehood?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "statehood"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: That they had been independent states before the creation of the kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that in the kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, within its borders there were no internal borders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were administrative borders. Yes, there were administrative borders internal to the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I know very well when the banovinas were formed, but I'm talking about the very inception of that kingdom. And I know that the banovinas were named after rivers and so on, but we can come to that later.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, even in 1918 to 1929, there were internal boundaries, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Between which entities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina was defined as an administrative unit in the constitution of 1921.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1921. I'm asking you in 1918. Let's say between 1918 and 1921, were there any internal borders?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think maybe we're confusing the term "internal borders," because the national government of Bosnia and Herzegovina did function in that period as an administrative unit and continued to do so after 1921. I don't want to suggest that that boundary between Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb or Croatian territories was an international boundary. It was not. But it was a designated administrative unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: No. Excuse me. That is not my question. I know what international borders are of the kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. My question to you was whether within these international borders, were there any other borders until the banovinas were introduced in 1921 or 1922, or whenever they were formed.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but can you tell me what you mean by "borders" or "boundaries"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's say something like this: What were the borders of Macedonia, if they existed, in 1918? Can you tell me, "This is where the border was and Macedonia brought in this," or you say, "Slovenia, there are the borders and this is the territory they brought into the union, and Croatia," and so on?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for Macedonia the answer is no, one cannot do that because those territories were acquired by Serbia in the Balkans in the wars. But in the case of Slovenia and in the case of Herzegovina, yes, one can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, let's move to the administrative division into banovinas. Can you tell us in which of the banovinas Bosanski Samac was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. It was on the -- it was right at the intersection of the three, but it was in -- I think it was the -- I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: It cannot be on the boundary. It has to be part of one of them. It is true that this was at the border of three banovinas. But since you mentioned it -- and for the record, let me suggest to you - and maybe you can agree on this - that it was in the Drina banovina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You touched on demographics a bit. Based on that, can you agree with me that according to the census - and let's start with the early ones in 1878, 1895, 1910, and the ones taken by the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and then the socialist Yugoslavia - that the Serbs were the most numerous nation in Bosnia and Herzegovina until the census of 1970?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you one more question based on your testimony this morning. Do you agree that the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, or at that point the Yugoslav army, for the most part had left the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 19th and 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, how long did the Yugoslav army stay in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- in my view, the troops of the units and the vast majority of the weaponry remained through until 1995 and simply underwent a name change in May of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. The next counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Donia, my name is Novak Lukic, and I will ask you questions on behalf of the Defence of the accused Miroslav Tadic. It will be a very few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I ask questions, with the permission of the Trial Chamber and regarding the objection I lodged regarding the exhibit C39 - and I don't know exactly how it was marked by the Registry - in case Mr. Donia does not dispute the date when this decision was adopted, I will withdraw the objection. I have in front of me a copy of the Official Gazette. And under number 386, this is the decision on the strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina for which it is stated that it was adopted on the 11th of May, 1992, and it is the same in the English version which is numbered 815457. I would just ask that Mr. Donia be shown the copy and check the date of 26 November 1993. And if he can state his view on this and if he can confirm this, then I would withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel is discussing a document marked P5, Exhibit P5. MR. LUKIC [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With simply one minor change. I think you mentioned the 11th of May. That date was the 12th of May that the assembly approved these six strategic objectives, according to this document, and I otherwise concur with the Official Gazette here as it states it. MR. LUKIC [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the decision was published in November 1993, in the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the Court's information, I believe the Gazette that was shown to the witness has not been marked. I only marked the one page of the English translation. So the Court may want to mark that also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel. You've got what the Prosecution is saying? MR. LUKIC [Interpretation] Yes. Of course I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because we only needed an agreement on the date when it was you published, can we only have an ID number, please, because there is no dispute. MR. LUKIC [Interpretation] Yes, the date of its publishing.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That shall be marked as ID1/3. MR. LUKIC [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, in the evidence you gave yesterday, you mentioned the propaganda of various parties when you were describing the backdrop of World War II and its consequences to the subsequent period. What I'm interested in is the form of the propaganda. What were the forms of this propaganda?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the propaganda that you're referring to as it appeared in 1990, 1991, in that period? Is that what -- your date of reference that you're asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm only asking about the forms of propaganda in that very period.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were various newspapers in which political leaders gave interviews. There were what we would recognise as editorial positions of some newspapers, a lot of speeches, even some placards and radio and television appearances by various leaders which promoted these viewpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did all three sides use such propaganda? When I say "three sides," I mean the three groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three national parties, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I noticed in your report that you mentioned as a source the daily newspaper Oslobodjenje on 25 different occasions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's about right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person named Hasan Cengic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him personally. I know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that in September 1991, he started acquiring weapons for Bosnia and Herzegovina through certain state organs of Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the name Mate Boban mean something to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the fact that on 27 December 1991, there were discussions with President Tudjman about a plan that an area comprising of 650.000 Croats be annexed to Croatia after having been proclaimed a separate entity?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, you did not find it useful to include these two facts in your report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I included the Herzegovinian -- Herceg-Bosna separatist declaration of 17 November 1991, did not reference the precedental transcript of the 27th of December, 1991. I did, in general, indicate that there were arming efforts going on by all nationalist formations in Bosnia in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You precisely described the discussions between Milosevic and Karadzic regarding the arming, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one more question. In your report, in paragraph 143, and in your yesterday's testimony, you mentioned the speech delivered by President Karadzic on the 15th of October, 1991 in the assembly house of Bosnia-Herzegovina when he threatened with physical extermination. And in your footnote related to this speech, you state that the presidents of political parties were allowed to address the deputies in the assembly. Do you know what Alija Izetbegovic stated before both houses of the parliament on the 27th of February, 1991?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 27th of February, 1991? I'm afraid not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will read this to you: "For the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I would sacrifice peace and -- I would never sacrifice sovereignty for peace." MR. LUKIC [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The fourth counsel, if any. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Madam President, Your Honours, after the very extensive testimony of Mr. Donia about the historical points of view, political points of view, I would suggest, and my line of questioning would be focused only to the period covered by the indictment, 1991 October and mostly 1992, I'd say, at the end of 1992, the period of political struggle in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then war and some other events specifically related to the region of Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Donia, just for the matter of clarification -- and the record shows that you are not in Merrill Lynch company?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct; I'm not. I'm not employed by Merrill Lynch.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you were at Merrill Lynch, you worked full time. You were in quite significant positions, such as vice-president. You worked as a financial consultant there. So my point is that you have worked there on a full-time basis.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. On the other hand, you were committed to certain historical research in Bosnia, and you performed these activities during your, I would say, free time and to some extent as a hobby, working with some of your friends from Bosnia, from America. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition, we could agree, couldn't we, that you are not a constitutional lawyer, you're not military expert, you're not a public international law expert?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct; I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And also, we could agree that you've never been in Samac, as you said this morning?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Have you visited the other area of Republika Srpska, the other entity of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you be so kind to tell us which area you visited?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited Banja Luka and Brcko and that kind of part of the corridor there between the two areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. Could you explain to us what was the purpose of your visit of this area of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- in the case of Brcko, I'd never seen one of the Sava River communities and I just wanted just to see it and visit. And in the case of Banja Luka, I went to a wedding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. So if I understand well - you can correct me, of course - you never performed any historical research or archive research or interview, or you didn't conduct any interview with the relevant political or military figures of Republika Srpska, of Bosnian Serbs in particular?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I bought some books, acquired some books, and did not do any interviews while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Donia, you didn't visit any official archive of Republika Srpska, parliament, Faculty of History, or military archive, or police, stuff like that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. Thank you, Mr. Donia. Mr. Donia, in your work -- in fact, it was the -- correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's paragraph 42 of Mr. Donia's report, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Speaking of the - at that time, in the middle of nineteenth century - of the, I would say, national doctrine or goals of Serbian nation, I repeat, in 1844, you, Mr. Donia, gave us quite interesting view, your personal view regard to that document. Have you been in possession or have you ever read this document with the title Nacertanije --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- of 1844? Sorry. Your answer was yes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Great. Thank you so much. This is good. So does the name Franjo Zah, F-r-a-n-g-o [sic], Z-a-h, mean something to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us just briefly about Franjo Zah, who was he, what he did.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franjo Zah was an agent of the Polish emigration who came to the area of the south Slav lands and visited first with Ljudevit Gaj in the drafting of a memorandum or plan, programme, which called for the creation of a south Slav state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. Now, could you tell me the relation between - of course, if you know - between British foreign office and Duke Catarinski and this agent Franjo Zah with regard to the idea of nacertanije and the policy of Serbia in the mid of nineteenth century?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that the British policy at that time at the Balkans was to some extent, and I would say more or less similar with the twentieth century, trying to prevent the influence of German and Austro-Hungarian Empire at that time? That approach would be correct or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, for your information, the policy of British foreign office, through Duke Catarinski and his agent Zah was to establish a big Serbia at that time, to have a community of south Slavs there, and to be a sort of buffer for the influence of Germany and Austria/Hungary at that time. This is a historical fact, and I'm very glad now that we too now are more familiar with that. Now my idea is to skip briefly, like in a time machine, to go to 1990, in the dome of the tragic events in Bosnia. 1990 was the year when the national parties of Bosnia organised elections and then they took certain positions in the government and the local communities too. Mr. Donia, would it be correct to say that in former Yugoslavia during the regime of Marshal Tito, as well as the period after his death until the first multiparty elections in Bosnia in 1990, in general terms, the principal of a national key was actually in the spot, in terms of the relations, internal politics, institutions, and bodies in the whole of Yugoslavia, with a rotation system, et cetera? Would it be correct to say that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In addition, would it be correct to say that in Bosnia, even more than the rest of Yugoslavia, this principle was followed very strictly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And probably you are familiar with the provisions of constitution of Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, I mean, prior to 1990.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you pointed out earlier, I'm not a constitutional specialist, and so I'd have to say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just on that very limited issue, Mr. Donia, about the so-called national equality key -- because you are very, very much familiar with the political life and the recent history in Bosnia. Just I'm speaking about the national key.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would agree that the national key was policy. As to the constitutional aspect of it, I can't comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. So are you familiar -- because why I'm asking you: You, in your paragraph 95 of your report, you're speaking -- as well as 93 and 94. But 95 is my focus now. You are speaking in quite details about the relations between ethnic groups in Bosnia at that time. You gave us a picture about the atmosphere in former Yugoslavia. So my idea and my next question would be: In your paragraph 95, you said that three major groups - Serbs, Croats, and Muslims - demanded a chamber of peoples. What did you mean by that, chamber of peoples? Because in your report, you want to assist this Honourable Trial Chamber, you want to assist the justice in general with your conclusions. And now you are, it seems to me, trying to present that you are not so familiar with these constitutions, but nevertheless you are mentioning these issues. So give us further details about your point of view, of course, about the constitutional picture in Bosnia at that time. Or we could delete your three paragraphs. I agree with that too, if you want.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if your question is what is a chamber of peoples, I can address that issue, because it was an institution that existed in the socialist period. And the composition of the chamber of peoples was of the three primary nationalities - Serbs, Croats, and Muslims - and each of those had designated numbers of deputies and they held the right to essentially call into question any legislation that would -- that was perceived by them to threaten the interests of one nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we could summarise that the principle of equality between three constitutive nations in Bosnia was in fact an issue, was in fact a fact, was in fact the situation in Bosnia. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Donia. Can you tell us, please: Do you know something about the amendments to the Bosnian constitution in 1990? Do you know -- do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that these amendments were enacted, were adopted, by the Bosnian Assembly and that they got into force, they were effective as of 31st July 1990?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two sets of amendments, one passed in 21st February and the other passed on the 31st of July, each of them effective at the date of their approval, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be correct to say that amendment numbered 70, 7-0, was in fact a constitutional framework for a chamber of people, of all three constitutive people of Bosnia, where the main task of this chamber was to protect the vital interest of each constitutive people in Bosnia at that time and, in addition, to prevent over-voting one constitutive nation, whoever it was at that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me and would want to look at that specific amendment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. I have, by chance, but it is in Serbian language, so Bosnian probably you cannot -- it cannot be of big help to you, but of course we shall provide it indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can I read, Your Honours, just this small piece so that Mr. Donia can give the answer about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. You can only do that if you promise that you are going to provide English translations to the Trial Chamber and to all the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's another problem, Madam President, because sometimes -- well, during my practice here at the Tribunal, the other party or Registry or Court management are not so willing to accept the translation provided by the Defence, so they're always making a double-check and another, I would say, second opinion. So this is a matter that I would like to raise during a convenient period for the Status Conference, just on these technical terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but then you have to accept that the Trial Chamber can only accept official translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Because we are not -- I mean, my experience told me that the version of translation coming from Defence were not recognised as official, so the question is whether we shall even proceed. Or maybe we could make a summary of the document in a few words, just to inform this Trial Chamber about it in general terms, allow the content of document, and then to proceed with official office for interpretation for you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I will allow you to ask the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just, Mr. Donia, a very -- I have a very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: On the condition that you're going to provide the translated copies later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, but now I will introduce that as the evidence. I have one copy for the Trial Chamber, and then I will provide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Translations later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Or the Trial Chamber will make the direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, sorry. This is the, I would say, housekeeping matters in terms of our proceedings, so I didn't want to take your time. Well, I will now read in Serbian language: "[Interpretation] In the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a council is hereby established to deal with the issue of implementation of equality of the nations and nationalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. An equal number of deputies shall be elected into the council from the ranks of each of the nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina - Muslims, Serbs, Croats - and an appropriate number of deputies from other ethnic groups or nationalities populating Bosnia and Herzegovina. Decisions shall be made by a two-third majority of the total number of deputies. Initiative for raising any issues before the Assembly shall be valid if 28 or more deputies believe that a certain issue from the competence of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, not a certain issue but a certain piece of legislation falling within the competence of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. " -- could infringe upon the principle of equality upon nations and nationalities."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Donia, could we agree upon the fact that certain mechanism of prevention of over-voting one constitutional nation in Bosnia actually was fully in accordance with the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your paragraph 108 -- although I'm not challenging actually, the paragraph and content of this paragraph. What I'm asking you: According to footnote 88, you said that the source for this information, which to some extent has some significant impact in the atmosphere of this particular trial, meaning the issue of international armed conflict, et cetera, et cetera -- so in your footnote 88, the only source for this very serious crisis was a newspaper called, Slobodna Bosna, Free Bosnia. And yesterday you told us that mostly you were relying on these sources for various reasons. So my question is: Do you have any other, I would say, more reliable source to say this is what was said in paragraph 100? Sorry, 108.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Or we are only dealing with the newspaper sources as a way to establish an expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- point out that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may re-read the statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no. Thank you, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in the sentence --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My question was very precise: Yes or no. Thank you. Let's go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We have lot of thing to do, Your Honours, here, and I really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- respecting the time and we are late.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is a cross-examination, Your Honours. It's not examination-in-chief. I don't want to hear any kind of historical forum or political forum --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- you are before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Madam President. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are under the orders of the Court --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- and the Court is here to control the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I absolutely concur with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If you see your counterpart on the floor, you stop talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My mistake. Excuse me. My apologies to my learned colleague from the Prosecution bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't believe the question was clear. It wasn't clear to me, and Dr. Donia was in the process of answering when he was cut off. There were several questions, I believe, contained in counsel's last remark he put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Madam President, I will rephrase my question to be more precise, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You rephrase your question and then allow the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, in light of the really shortage of time and in our proceedings, please answer me with yes or no. Did you consult any other reliable source than the source that you are referring in your footnote 88 in your report of paragraph 108? Please, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listed the other sources that I looked at in this paragraph, and the reason that that statement reads as it does is I simply state it was later reported. I do not claim this to be a fact that I have concluded as a verified piece of evidence. I simply recite the fact that it was reported in this particular newspaper. The other sources that I looked at were the memoirs of Professor Kecmanovic, and there was a statement also regarding this in the memoirs of Professor Pejanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. Now, in your paragraph 124, you are speaking about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, frankly, Your Honours, I could not say that Mr. Donia is speaking. He's trying to establish an interpretation which I found that it's very dubious.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For example, Mr. Donia, about the SAO district, the Serbian autonomous district, could you tell us, please, to what extent your knowledge as an historian is getting about the constitutional issues for formation of local communities in the region, in the regional assembly, in regional association of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I heard a couple of questions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The question is: You're an historian. You're dealing to some extent with some of the constitutional issues, constitutional law issues here. So you visited many times Bosnia. You wrote two books at least, a lot of articles. You participated in many of trials here, I think three or two here within this Tribunal. So tell us, are you familiar with the constitutional possibilities for municipalities to create a region in Bosnia? Yes or no, simply.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So that possibility was absolutely provided and enacted in Bosnian constitution. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you find then or could we agree that the Serbian -- association of Serbian municipalities at that time were fully in accordance with the principle that we have just discussed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So could you give me a comment on the following. This is the Article of 274 of Bosnian Constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, before you read the section --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Not all articles, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is a Constitution which was in force in 1990 in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: 1990 until 1992, actually when the armed conflict was under-place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Speaking about the regionalisation, and then -- I will speak in Serbian. [Interpretation] [As read] Article 275: "For the purpose of implementing a lasting cooperation, the municipalities whose territories are interlinked or contiguous may join each other to establish urban or regional communities. Those joined municipalities or those integrated municipalities shall reach agreement to determine the types of affairs which within their rights and obligations they shall entrust to the community. They shall also establish common bodies, join resources, adopt common plans for development, and conduct other affairs of common interest. "The conclusions and the positions of the communities obligate municipalities to adopt them in the assemblies of joined municipalities." [Previous translation continues]... [In English] in all your years of research, are you been familiar with -- I'm speaking about the territory of Bosnia. Have you been aware of this form of association in your research, in your period of visiting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm just a little confused of how the Court plans to treat these documents read by counsel. They're not marked, although I presume counsel is reading the Constitution correctly. I don't know which copy he has, and we don't ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I asked him for which year, and then we will have it marked when he finishes with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I did already tell him that on condition that he gives the English translations as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. My suggestion would be to deal with these technical issues after the testimony of this witness with regard to the interpretation, translation, and other things. It's a technical issue, so let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But I'm ready to provide a copy for the Trial Chamber, a copy for the Prosecutor bench, as well as, if necessary, for Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the -- yeah, this is interesting. Mr. Donia, this is really interesting. You know, speaking about -- about the parliamentary life in Bosnia and also relation between Serbia at that time and Bosnia, we are quite happy, Your Honours, to have two very important and key figures with us, although in Detention Unit, Mr. Krajisnik, who was a speaker of Bosnian parliament, and then Mr. Milosevic. Then probably on the basis of proprio motu or maybe a joint request or maybe subpoena might be issued for the certain persons and to give us more a profound, and I would say, direct testimony, but that's another issue. Mr. Donia, in your paragraph 143 of your report, you mentioned in your first expression that: "... majority of Bosnian assembly delegates, primarily from HDZ and SDA," being Croat and Muslim parties, "approved a resolution proclaiming the `sovereignty'..." My question, Mr. Donia, would be: Would this quotation of word "sovereignty" of B and H, practically what did you mean by quotation of word "sovereignty"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the -- by putting it in quotes, I simply meant to suggest that that's what it's typically called in all references that I've seen of it, the resolution on sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Great. So we are not misunderstanding this grammatical form that sovereignty with the quotation was used in sort of an ironic or maybe similar term? It's not ironic. I mean, it's not kind of -- speaking about sovereignty, you --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not satire, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, in fact, you're speaking about a real sovereignty, real document, about real issue sovereignty, or you have some doubts about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I allude to the title of the resolution, and that's what I mean to do in this sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Without concluding that this is sovereignty in terms of public international law or doctrine of public international law? So you just make a reference to the declaration of sovereignty of B and H, sort of, say, for the local use, for internal use?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me be clear. I do not suggest or imply that this is a conclusion that I reach on the basis of international law. I simply here refer to the common title by which this resolution is known and of which you gave me the correct date yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Donia. And then in paragraph 144, you are speaking about the Assembly of Serbian People of B and H. Could we say that the same applies to this body, meaning Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Same approach. You said that with quotation of "sovereignty," you were referring to the declaration of sovereignty as it is, without getting any conclusions insofar. So the same approach would be applied for the word or for the name "Assembly of Serbian People of B and H" --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- as a factually.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used the term here in the same -- I used the quotation marks because it's the first time in this paragraph that I introduce this title.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Donia. Good. Now, Your Honours, and, Mr. Donia, we are in paragraph 148. We have again quotation marks for the word "preparations" now. Why is that? "Preparations." "Preparations" meaning what? Is this sort of institution or sort of process or undisputed fact? Could you explain us now these quotation marks in paragraph 148?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reference note 136 here and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can I -- do you need the --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm simply quoting --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Footnote 136. Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the resolution of the Serbian Assembly as it appeared in the newspaper Oslobodjenje, in my translation, and I will grant you that is not an authorised Tribunal translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but still, you didn't answer my question. Word "preparation" with quotation marks following the, I would say, same practice with the previous two, could we consider as a fact or a quotation from the newspaper or maybe your expert opinion? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the newspaper carried the text of the resolution, so this would be a one-word excerpt from the newspaper publication as it appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Donia, let us deal with the paragraph 154 of your report. In particular, I would like to make reference to again quotation, but now with italic letters, "prepare to take-over." Serious issue. Could you tell us, what does it mean? Did you find this, I would say, a process, or did you find, let's say, traces of these activities in this so-called plan A/B, or it's just your personal assumption or conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The phrase that I've quoted here, "prepare the take-over," I quote from and it is italicised in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the document. I do believe, and my colleagues can confirm, that we have a very detailed check of this document. There is no such word in the document. But now, just as a matter of clarification, in paragraph 158 --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. That statement was just made, and it's not accurate. The document on page 6 in my translation carries in italics "prepare the take-over of staff and selected equipment of security service centres," if it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. We don't have this. Now, let's speak, Mr. Donia, about your assumption in paragraph 158. It seems to me that there are some, well, misinterpretation in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is not so serious issue. It's rather -- I don't know. In Serbian language, the word "shooting," which is -- "... ostensibly in protest against the shooting of a Serb at wedding ..." I don't know. What is the name in Serbian version of -- to the best my knowledge, in Serbian version that was "wounding," wounding of a Serb at the Serb wedding. And then "shooting," just as matter of qualification, what was that, killing, shooting, wounding, or something else?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Let's go to the other paragraph. Good. It's interesting. Paragraph 166. You said in your paragraph: "The importance of conquest and cleansing became starkly evident in the peace agreement that ended the Croatian war signed on 2nd January," et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. "The territorial division followed closely the lines of confrontation and interposed UN peacekeeping forces between the rival military forces while providing for a reversal of ethnic cleansing only at the future date," et cetera, et cetera. Now, Mr. Donia, we are facing a very serious international law issue. You speak -- you're speaking in your paragraph 166 about the position of UN peacekeepers, about the former policy -- of the policy of former Secretary of State, Mr. Vance, and then about the peace agreement between Croatia, and war. To some extent, you are trying to present a conclusion about the ethnic cleansing in relation with the actions of UN peacekeepers and other parts of the ethnic community. So my question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before the question is posed, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could just ask the Court if the Court could direct counsel to ask questions rather than -- he can argue Dr. Donia's qualifications at a proper time, at the end of the case, but these were all arguments prior to - I see counsel's about to ask a question - but prior to this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, my dear colleague. I just want to save the time of this Trial Chamber. So I'm not reading all the paragraph. I'm just referring to certain relevant parts, and then I will -- I'm trying to establish my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Pantelic. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Regarding your, I would say, theory in this paragraph 166, would it be fair to say that the same theory or same approach, your professional personal approach, would be applied to a case of Cyprus, where we have two divided community under the supervision of UN peacekeepers? So my question is: This situation and your idea in this paragraph, could it be like to the case of Cyprus? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't thought about it. I'm not certain. I couldn't give you an answer right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, you are speaking about Samac area. You told us today and yesterday that you've never been in Samac, you never consulted Republika Srpska archives, you have never consulted your colleagues, Serbian experts, or, you know, question -- the person in question, et cetera. And still, you are speaking about the atmosphere of -- in your chapter related to Samac, from paragraph - I will not refer to in particular - from 157 until, including -- until the end of your report, which is the paragraph - just a moment - which is the paragraph 188. First of all, I have an impression, after reading your report with paragraph 188 -- could you tell us why you suddenly ceased to -- why you suddenly stopped with your report? Last sentence: "In the view of the army command, the leadership of Bosanski Samac municipality was a model for others in the RS to emulate." Isn't it really a bit strange that the expert is finishing his opinion, his report, only, you know, just suddenly, without any sort of general summary or conclusion or stuff? I mean, just a matter of style. I would like to ask you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The question is: Are you always in your work give this form of report, without conclusion or short summary or something? Because to me, it seems that it's, you know, by accident it was stopped here, like you didn't have enough time, maybe toner in your computer or some other technical stuff. It was just cut. You know, your line of -- it's my impression. Correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't share your characterisation of the report. I think your original question was: Do I finish all my work this way?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer would be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. Speaking about ethnic cleansing and your personal approach to that issue, are you familiar with the cases of ethnic cleansing of Bosnian Serbs in other area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, meaning the area under the control of Bosnian Muslim forces and Bosnian Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that certain ethnic cleansing and wars against humanity committed against the Serbs occurred in Bosnia and Herzegovina during civil war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are you aware how many refugees, Bosnian Serb refugees, came to Samac region in the time of war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. Would it be fair to say, Mr. Donia, that some very high-ranked Muslim officials in fact tried to initiate the form of persecution among their own compatriots, preparing for a false picture, and then trying to establish the atmosphere of persecution of Bosnian Muslims under the direction of Bosnian Muslim authorities in order to provoke a reaction of western community against Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good. Now, Mr. Donia, I would like --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Luckily, Your Honours, I have translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would like to introduce -- I don't know exactly what is the ID number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which document is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have a -- in fact, this is officially, yes, for the -- I have for all members of this Trial Chamber one document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is that the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. This is a document that just now I will speak about, and this is for our learned colleague from the Prosecutor bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, can we have the ID number for --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. You can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- the Constitution, the one you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You can see what the number will be, sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you number this one, can we have the number for the Constitution, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And this is the last question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Let's straighten up the documents. Can we have the ID number first for the constitution which you referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the ID number for the Constitution shall be ID1/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In fact, the -- sorry. Do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And then this document he is just --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I provided three copies for Madam President and members of Trial Chamber, Your Honours, for the Honourable Judge, and one copy for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is -- can you first describe it? What is the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can describe. Well, this is the instruction of Muslim party, the main headquarters of Muslim party in Sarajevo, sending an instruction to a branch office party in Trebinje, Muslim party in Trebinje, which is the south of Bosnia, number 5293, date January 20th, 1993, and references, instructions, concerning the moving out from Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So Muslim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before you pose your question, can I hear from the Prosecution? Do they have this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I haven't received it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no. I gave a copy for my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I gave three, four. Trial Chamber, one for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please, can you assist. Can you get the copy from counsel to give to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry. That was my impression, that I provided with enough ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we give time for the Prosecution to look at it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To see whether they've had it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Madam President, we have all the time in this world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a document and a translation of that. Apparently it was faxed to a law office. I don't know what the source of it is. I'm not -- I don't believe that the authenticity of it has been established. I wouldn't be prepared to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe since this is 1.00, we can adjourn until tomorrow morning. In the meantime, the parties can discuss this document and see whether or not there would be any objection from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, until the document is verified by the Prosecution so that they can --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I concur with you. Sorry. Pardon me, Your Honour. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't have a question, but I would like -- regarding the evidence, but I'd like to ask the Chamber this: Before I -- well, obviously we're drawing to a close with this witness and we will be ready to call the next witness tomorrow morning. There will be no problem with that, of course. Before we do so, would that be an appropriate time to deal with the outstanding motions? I ask that because it's a natural break in the flow of evidence, and if the Chamber wants -- is amenable to that suggestion, it would be, I think, useful for all counsel to know if you propose to do that. Because I would also like to address -- A, deal with the motions; and B, address the Chamber briefly on the issue, the general issue of documentary evidence and its introduction, before I start the witness. So I respectfully ask the Chamber to indicate its views with respect to the matters I raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will deal with that tomorrow morning, after completing this witness. So we are adjourning, and then the document which the counsel was about to ask questions on can be discussed between the parties. The Prosecution can verify whatever they have to say about it before it is put to the witness tomorrow morning. Yes. And after we are through with the witness, after he is released, then we will deal with the motions. Some motions -- some decisions have already been filed, some others will be given orally. So the first 10, 15 minutes tomorrow, I mean after this witness has gone, before the next witness is called, we'll deal with motions, but the witness must be brought. MR. DI FAZIO: Can I also indicate -- oh, yes, of course we will be ready to go. Do you mean into Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. Within the building. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Immediately available. He will be here just outside of Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. After this witness is released, we will deal with motions or any other matters that counsel, both sides, wish to address the Court on. After we've finished, then the witness, the next witness, will be brought into Court. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other matters counsel wish to say? We shall adjourn until tomorrow morning at 0930 hours. The Court will rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
